- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.75) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5% relative to historical mean or recent 7-day average.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model often underestimates or lags; adjust forecast upward by 1–3% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior 7-day high), model frequently overshoots; cap forecast at 10–15% below peak or use 30-day moving average as ceiling.
- If sentiment turns sharply negative mid-period, model often fails to correct downward; apply downward bias of 1–3% per day of negative sentiment exposure.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to overreact to short-term sentiment swings; use sentiment-weighted smoothing (e.g., 70% recent, 30% 30-day average) to dampen noise.
- When sentiment is neutral (0.33–0.67), model often exhibits mean reversion bias; align forecast toward 30-day moving average or 14-day exponential smoother.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “reversal” patterns (e.g., bullish → bearish → bullish), model tends to mispredict direction; use sentiment momentum (last 3 sentiment values) to adjust directionality bias.
